sections.title: How does the Diffraction grating calculator work?
sections.html:
The Diffraction grating calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports grating density in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the first order, the second order and the third order.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Diffraction grating calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Grating density=(the sine of (angle of incidence) + the sine of (first order)) ÷ wavelength
Grating density=(1 ÷ 2) × (the sine of (angle of incidence) + the sine of (second order)) ÷ wavelength
Grating density=(1 ÷ 3) × (the sine of (angle of incidence) + the sine of (third order)) ÷ wavelength
Grating density=(1 ÷ 4) × (the sine of (angle of incidence) + the sine of (fourth order)) ÷ wavelength
Grating density=(1 ÷ 5) × (the sine of (angle of incidence) + the sine of (fifth order)) ÷ wavelength

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Wavelength = 30 nm, Angle of incidence = 10 deg and First order = 10 deg. Working through the relationship above gives Grating density = 115.7655 mm, Second order = 31.3956 deg, Third order = 60.2549 deg and Fourth order = 90 deg.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Grating density = 115.7655 mm, Second order = 31.3956 deg, Third order = 60.2549 deg and Fourth order = 90 deg should be roughly the size you expected from Wavelength = 30 nm and Angle of incidence = 10 deg.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Diffraction grating calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the first order, the second order and the third order — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

faq.q: What does the Diffraction grating calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns grating density, derived from the first order, the second order and the third order. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Diffraction grating calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the first order, the second order and the third order, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter wavelength in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Wavelength opens in nanometers and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Grating density = 115.7655 mm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Diffraction grating calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
